title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal worst-case number of synchronous communication rounds for randomized triangle detection on arbitrary simple undirected networks with \(n\) vertices. Each directed use of an edge carries at most \(\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits per round. On a triangle-free input every vertex must output NO; on any input containing a triangle at least one vertex must output YES. Require this joint correctness event to have probability at least \(15/16\) on every input and identifier assignment. Seek a positive asymptotic rate \(F(n)\), a uniform algorithm with round bound \(O(F(n))\), and a matching \(\Omega(F(n))\) lower bound for every correct uniform algorithm in the model below. Polylogarithmic factors are part of the target.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
definitions:
An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge3\), including disconnected graphs and isolated vertices. A triangle consists of three distinct vertices with all three edges present. Each vertex has a distinct integer identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). Initially a vertex knows \(n\), its own identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors. Its incident edges also have distinct local port numbers from one to its degree; the ports at opposite endpoints need not agree. Correctness and time bounds range over every graph, every identifier assignment and every port numbering.

All vertices run one finite classical program, the same for all sizes and vertices. They have independent private fair random bits and no advice, global random tape or preprocessing. In each synchronous round a vertex performs a finite local computation and sends a separate message to each neighbor. Messages have exactly \(b(n)=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with padding permitted, and are received before the next round. There is no other communication channel. Local computation and storage are unbounded but terminate between rounds on every random tape. Fixing this bandwidth coefficient removes an unspecified model constant; a fixed larger coefficient can be simulated by a constant number of rounds.

Every vertex eventually halts and emits one bit, interpreted as YES or NO. It need not exhibit a triangle, and a vertex emitting YES need not belong to a triangle. Halting vertices can subsequently send a fixed dummy message. The global output is the disjunction of the local bits. In particular, a negative input requires all bits to be zero on the successful event, while a positive input only requires at least one bit to be one. Information about a remote triangle need not reach every connected component.

For an algorithm \(A\), let \(T_A(n)\) be the maximum number of rounds until all vertices halt, over inputs of exactly \(n\) vertices, legal identifiers and ports, and all random tapes. Eligible algorithms must have finite \(T_A(n)\) for every \(n\) and the stated success probability on every instance. This is a worst-case round bound, not expected time. The class is nonempty, for example by transmitting finite adjacency information along edges using sufficiently many rounds.

A matching rate means a function \(F:\{3,4,\ldots\}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), one eligible algorithm \(A\), a constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(n_0\) with \(T_A(n)\le C F(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\); and, for each eligible algorithm \(B\), constants \(c_B>0\) and \(n_B\) with \(T_B(n)\ge c_B F(n)\) for every \(n\ge n_B\). Lower-bound constants may depend on the fixed program but not on input size. A solution must give an independently specified asymptotic rate and establish both bounds, rather than merely defining the optimum by minimization over algorithms. The absolute-error convention for numerical values does not replace these asymptotic quantifiers.

The success threshold \(15/16\) is a precise editorial choice matching the checked lower-bound theorem. It is not asserted here that distributed disjunctive output at success \(2/3\) can automatically be amplified by a constant number of independent repetitions: different repetitions may report YES at different vertices.

progress.text: The near-optimal enumeration algorithm also detects triangles in \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) rounds with high probability. Its upper-bound role is corroborated in the checked 2025 introduction; the full 2021 proof was not re-audited.
Theorem 1 and the proof of Result 1 give the \(\Omega(\log\log n)\) lower bound with success at least \(15/16\). The card now records that exact error convention.
The ADGA survey retains the complexity of detection as open and distinguishes it from listing.

context_blocks.text: A vertex already knows its incident edges, but still needs information about edges between its neighbors. Short edge messages limit how quickly that missing information can be collected.
Enumeration must distribute all witnesses, while detection only needs a positive report somewhere. Consequently, a matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the detection rate.

The 2025 argument gets beyond one-round impossibility using information-theoretic techniques. The large remaining gap is the target; the precise success requirement matters because local reports are combined by disjunction.

answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of a rate \(F\) with both quantified bounds above, including correctness and the worst-case round analysis of one uniform randomized algorithm and an unconditional lower bound against all eligible algorithms. Suppressing unknown logarithmic factors, proving only a listing lower bound, or establishing only one side is partial progress. A result with a different output convention, communication graph, success threshold or expected-time guarantee must include a proved reduction preserving the required asymptotic rate.

importance.reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.

sentences: A distributed network must detect whether three vertices are pairwise adjacent.
Every edge carries only logarithmically many bits per synchronous round.
A positive input needs one YES report somewhere, and the joint answer must be correct with probability at least fifteen sixteenths.
The target is matching upper and lower round bounds, including any logarithmic factors.
Known detection bounds remain far apart, and the stronger output requirement of listing triangles does not close that gap.
